items.title: Reform or legislative overreach? How Maharashtra's amendment to its public trusts law reached Tata Sons' governance
items.summary: In 2025, Maharashtra amended its public trusts law to limit the number of lifetime trustees where a trust’s governing instrument does not specifically provide for their appointment, a change that has placed some of India’s largest business houses, whose controlling shareholders are public trusts in Maharashtra, under regulatory scrutiny. A trust is a fiduciary arrangement whereby a settlor transfers property to a trustee to hold and manage for the benefit of beneficiaries. Private trusts, created for ascertainable individuals or classes, are governed by the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and give the settlor considerable autonomy over trustee appointments, distribution of benefits and the trust’s operation. Public trusts, created for charitable or religious purposes benefiting the public, are regulated by state legislation and attract greater oversight. Even so, the settlor’s intentions, as expressed in the trust deed, remain paramount. The State’s role has traditionally been supervisory, ensuring the trust’s objects are honoured and preventing misfeasance, malfeasance and non-feasance rather than interventionist in the selection and composition of trustees. items.title: AI liability and regulation for India's GCCs
items.summary: India’s Global Capability Centres (“ GCCs ”) have evolved significantly from their traditional back-office functions. They are increasingly developing and deploying generative and agentic AI, not to mention adopting the use of AI in several functions. The use of AI may raise questions under data protection, intellectual property, employment, consumer protection, cybersecurity and sector-specific laws, while the nature of the system itself may raise separate questions about autonomy, human oversight, decision-making and accountability. A GCC therefore needs to assess both the legal framework applicable to a particular AI system and the how it operates. An AI tool that assists an employee in a GCC to prepare a recommendation is different from a system that independently makes decisions and acts. Consequently, the risks associated with each also differ. Justice Nagarathna was delivering the opening remarks at the National Annual Stakeholders Consultation marking ten years of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, held at the Supreme Court. Highlighting the challenges surrounding the treatment of children accused of serious offences, Justice Nagarathna observed, "The question of treating a child in conflict with law as an adult represents one of the most delicate fault lines in our criminal justice system." She emphasised that juvenile justice boards (JJBs) were not intended to function as miniature criminal courts and that the law recognised children's capacity for development and change. items.title: Is there a right time to go in-house?
items.summary: For many attorneys, moving in-house is seen as a natural progression in a legal career. After spending several years in private practice, the opportunity to work closely with a business, take ownership of legal and business issues, and become part of commercial decision-making can be compelling. However, the decision is often framed around when to leave private practice, rather than what an attorney should have built before making the move. While an in-house role can offer a different kind of exposure and responsibility, the transition also represents a significant shift in the way an attorney works. The skills and experience that are valuable in private practice may not always be the same as those required in-house. This raises an important question: Is there a right time to go in-house? Answer: There is no single point in a lawyer's career that can be considered the right time to move in-house. The answer depends on the lawyer’s experience, the nature of the role and, importantly, what they are looking to achieve from the move. items.title: Why power banks in hold luggage pose such a risk
items.summary: Airline passengers are being warned not to pack power banks in their hold luggage ahead of the summer holiday travel period. Devices with rechargeable batteries, like mobile phones, laptops, tablets, and smartwatches can be plugged into power banks on the go, where charging sockets may not be available. However, power banks are not danger-free or environmentally friendly. The warning has come from the UK’s Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), which believes that many travellers still aren’t aware of the rules – or the fire risk. Passengers on UK flights must take power banks – and other items containing lithium batteries – with them into the cabin. They must never be used to charge another electronic device while on the plane. Additionally, only two power banks per person are allowed on a flight. Consider a scenario where you are about to take off on a flight. You have settled into your seat, started using your mobile phone, and put it in airplane mode. All of a sudden, an unusual hissing sound comes from your bag; smoke starts rising, and within seconds, there is a fire inside your luggage. items.title: Eerie calm to the violence of lathis: Walking through Delhi on October 9 and 10
items.summary: On October 9, as the sun gently set over central Delhi, the city fell into an unusually quiet lull. It was the day before the protests demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and a rollback of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. If it weren’t so dystopian, it might have been called calm. The road leading to the protest site at Jantar Mantar had been barricaded at both ends. New surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees every few hundred metres. From the speakers, a woman’s voice, unhurried and polite, warned people not to join the next day’s demonstration. Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita was in force, she said. Gatherings of five or more, slogans, and protest symbols were prohibited. Then the message played again, and again, in a continuous loop. Closer to Jantar Mantar, a policeman stood over a labourer as he welded four rows of metal barricades into one, so that no protester could drag them apart. items.title: The climate trouble on India’s roads
items.summary: Bengaluru-based writer and educationist Chandrika R. Krishnan has made five visits to the mountains in North India in the last decade. And each time, her road journeys have gotten delayed because of landslides. “I remember waiting it out in Kashmir, Ladakh and Uttarakhand because rainfall-triggered landslides had temporarily blocked the road,” Krishnan told ISignal . Some of these visits were outside the monsoon window. Krishnan visited Leh and Ladakh in August 2019, Char Dham (the four sacred Hindu Himalayan shrines) in May 2022, Amarnath and Kashmir in May 2024, Adi Kailash in June 2025, and Vaishno Devi in October 2025. While hilly roads are known to be prone to landslides, studies show that road construction—which the Himalayan region (and India as a whole) has seen a lot of in the last decade —can contribute to both their frequency and magnitude. In March 2025, researchers published a landslide susceptibility map for an 80-km stretch from Karnaprayag to Joshimath in Uttarakhand along National Highway 7, a mountainous corridor connecting Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
